sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Sacubitril/valsartan is being investigated for cardiac protection during cancer therapy. However, evidence regarding its preventive effect on cancer therapy–related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD) remains inconsistent.

sec.title: Aims
sec.p: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of sacubitril/valsartan for the prevention of CTRCD during oncologic therapy.

sec.title: Methods and results
sec.p: We searched PubMed, EMBASE, and Web of Science for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing sacubitril/valsartan with control for the prevention of CTRCD during oncologic therapy, with treatment effects synthesized using risk ratio (RR), mean differences (MD), or standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals.

Four RCTs involving 410 participants were included. Sacubitril/valsartan reduced the absolute risk of CTRCD compared with control (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.82, p < 0.001). Sacubitril/valsartan was associated with a significant improvement in left ventricular ejection fraction (MD 1.19%, 95% CI 0.05 to 2.33, p = 0.045), global longitudinal strain (SMD 0.43, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.75, p = 0.026), and a reduction in troponin (log-MD − 0.43, 95% CI − 0.59 to − 0.26, p < 0.001), compared with the control group. Sacubitril/valsartan increased the risk of hypotension (RR 4.75, 95% CI 1.78 to 12.63, p = 0.002). No significant differences were observed in left ventricular volume, work indices, or NT-proBNP levels. Trial sequential analysis indicated that the current evidence remains insufficient to draw firm conclusions regarding the effect of cardioprotection on CTRCD.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Sacubitril/valsartan may be associated with modest reductions in CTRCD risk and attenuation of LVEF and GLS decline in patients with preserved baseline cardiac function receiving chemotherapy. However, the clinical relevance remains inconclusive when considering the trial sequential analysis and the modest magnitude of effect. These findings are primarily hypothesis-generating rather than practice-changing, and require confirmation in larger randomized trials, particularly in higher-risk populations.

Trial sequential analysis indicated that the current evidence remains insufficient to confirm a definitive treatment effect

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The advances in cancer treatment has improved the outcome of cancer, however, cancer therapy related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD) emerges as a new problem [1]. CTRCD is characterized by wide range of clinical presentations from elevation in biomarker asymptomatic decrease in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) or Global longitudinal strain (GLS) to severe symptomatic heart failure [2]. Cancer therapy–induced heart failure is associated with an adverse prognosis, with mortality rates comparable to those observed in other forms of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy [3]. Therefore, early recognition and prompt management, including primary prevention, is warranted.

Many cancer therapies, including anthracyclines and the monoclonal antibody trastuzumab, can induce cardiac dysfunction through multiple mechanisms: excessive reactive oxygen species generation, topoisomerase II–mediated DNA damage, mitochondrial injury, and inhibition of cardioprotective signaling pathways such as HER2 [4]. The prevention of CTRCD has been approached by targeting these specific pathogenic mechanisms related to cancer therapies or by modulating common maladaptive neurohormonal pathways [5].

Current guidelines recommend primary preventive strategies for patients at high or very high baseline risk of CTRCD. Renin–angiotensin system inhibitors, beta-blockers, and statins are recommended based on evidence from studies of moderate sample size, demonstrating modest treatment effects [2, 5]. A recent meta-analysis demonstrated that angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ACEI/ARB) were associated with a non-significant mean difference of 1.5% in LVEF change compared with control, whereas beta-blockers showed a more pronounced effect (mean difference, 2.4%).As a component of contemporary standard heart failure treatment, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors (ARNI) have been evaluated in this setting; however, the results have been inconsistent. Although the Sacubitril/Valsartan for the Prevention of Anthracycline Cardiotoxicity in Patients With Elevated Cardiac Troponin I Concentration During Chemotherapy (SARAH) trial and studies by Katogiannis et al. and Hsu et al. suggest a protective role of ARNI against CTRCD, the Prevention of Cardiac Dysfunction During Adjuvant Breast Cancer Therapy II (PRADA II) trial failed to demonstrate a significant preventive effect of ARNI therapy [6–9]. These inconsistent findings highlight the need for a comprehensive synthesis of the available evidence. Accordingly, given the conflicting results of current RCTs, we conducted this meta-analysis to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of prophylactic ARNI therapy for the prevention of CTRCD in cancer patients with normal baseline cardiac function.

sec.title: Method
sec.p: We conducted this systematic review and meta-analysis in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The research question was formulated using the Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcomes (PICO) framework (Supplementary Table 1). The study protocol was prospectively registered in the PROSPERO database (Registration ID: CRD420251243920).

sec.title: Data source and search strategy
sec.p: We systematically searched PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), together with major clinical trial registry databases, from database inception to December 31, 2025, without restriction on language. To identify additional eligible studies, we manually screened the reference lists of all included trials, relevant review articles, and prior meta-analyses. The detailed search strategy is provided in Supplementary Table 2.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: Studies were eligible if they were (1) RCTs comparing sacubitril/valsartan with standard care and (2) reported CTRCD or left ventricular functional parameters assessed at baseline and at follow-up. Left ventricular function could be assessed by echocardiography or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR). Potentially eligible studies were independently screened by two investigators (Y.J.W. and C.S.H.). Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus, with adjudication by a third reviewer (H.J.L.) when necessary.

sec.title: Data extraction and quality assessment
sec.p: Two investigators (Y.J.W. and C.S.H.) independently extracted data from all eligible studies. The extracted variables included publication year, country, study year, eligibility criteria, baseline demographic and clinical characteristics, and follow-up duration. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus, with adjudication by a third reviewer (H.J.L.) when needed. As this study involved the synthesis of previously published data, ethical approval was not required. The risk of bias for all included RCTs was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool.

sec.title: Endpoints
sec.p: The primary endpoint was CTRCD, defined according to criteria consistent with the 2022 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) cardio-oncology guidelines when applicable [2]. When definitions used in the trial were not fully aligned with the 2022 ESC cardio-oncology criteria, the primary endpoint as defined in the original trial was adopted. In particular, definition incorporating GLS was retained due to the higher sensitivity of GLS to detect early LV dysfunction. Key secondary endpoints were the changes from baseline (post-treatment minus baseline) in LVEF, GLS, and serum cardiac troponin levels (cardiac troponin T or I). Exploratory endpoints were the changes of LV volume indices, myocardial work indices, NT-proBNP, systolic and diastolic blood pressures. The safety endpoint was the incidence of hypotension, as defined in each included trial. Detailed definitions and measurement methods for each endpoint are summarized in Supplementary Table 3.

sec.title: Data synthesis and statistical analysis
sec.p: Meta-analyses were conducted in accordance with the recommendations of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. For binary outcomes, including CTRCD and hypotension, effect sizes were estimated using risk ratios (RR). Bayesian model estimating risk ratios were additionally applied as sensitivity analyses for binary outcomes to assess the robustness of the results.

For continuous endpoints, pooled effect estimates were calculated using effect measures appropriate to the scale and distribution of each variable. Mean differences were used for LVEF, left ventricular volumes, myocardial work indices and blood pressures, as these outcomes were reported on consistent measurement scales across studies. Standardized mean differences (SMD) were applied for global longitudinal strain (GLS) to account for inter-vendor and inter-software variability in GLS measurement and reporting across studies [10, 11]. Serum biomarkers, including cardiac troponin and N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), were logarithmically transformed prior to analysis to address skewed distributions, and pooled using mean differences of log-transformed values. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate the influence of clinical heterogeneity, including differences in participant characteristics and treatment regimens. These analyses included the systematic exclusion of individual studies and assessed the consistency of treatment effects across both efficacy and safety endpoints.

Subgroup analyses were conducted according to HER2 status, when endpoint data were available. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using τ2 and I2. Publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger’s regression test when the number of available studies was sufficient.

Trial sequential analysis (TSA) was performed to assess the robustness of the cumulative evidence, with adjustment for diversity (D²). The required information size was calculated assuming a two-sided type I error of 5%, 80% power, and a relative risk reduction of 30% (RR = 0.70). O’Brien–Fleming α-spending boundaries and non-binding futility boundaries were applied, and the cumulative Z-curve was plotted against these thresholds. All statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.5.0).

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: The initial literature search identified 263 records (108 from PubMed, 74 from EMBASE, 38 from Web of Science, 20 from the CENTRAL, and 23 from clinical trial registries). After removing 77 duplicate records and screening titles and abstracts, eleven articles were retrieved for full-text assessment. Of these, seven studies were excluded for the following reasons: inappropriate study design or protocol (n = 3), meta-analyses or review articles (n = 2), abstract-only publications (n = 1), and inclusion of participants with baseline heart failure (n = 1) (Fig. 1). Finally, four studies involving a total of 410 patients met the eligibility criteria and were included in the systematic review and quantitative meta-analysis [6–9].

sec.title: Study description
sec.p: The clinical characteristics of the four included RCTs are summarized in Table 1. One trial (PRADA II) was a multi-center study conducted in Norway [8], whereas the other 3 trials were single-center studies conducted in Brazil, Greece and Taiwan [6, 7, 9]. The mean age of participants ranged from 46.7 to 54.1 years, with 88.5% being female. Two studies included only patients with breast cancer [7, 8], while the SARAH trial enrolled patients receiving anthracycline-based therapy, of whom approximately 80% had breast cancer [9]. The remaining study (Katogiannis et al.) enrolled patients with hematologic malignancies undergoing bone marrow transplantation [6]. Given its distinct clinical context compared with the other 3 included studies, sensitivity analyses excluding this study were subsequently performed for the endpoints when applicable.

sec.p: Patients with heart failure at baseline were excluded from all four studies [6–9] Only one trial required elevation of cardiac troponin (> 99th percentile) as an inclusion criteria [9]. Baseline cardiovascular risk was generally at low to moderate level across the study populations. In the study by Hsu et al., 98% (98/100) of participants were classified as low to moderate risk according to the Heart Failure Association–International Cardio-Oncology Society (HFA-ICOS) score [7], and in the SARAH study, 97.3% (109/112) were categorized as low to moderate risk [9]. In the study by Katogiannis et al., cardiovascular risk was assessed using the Cardiac Risk in Bone Marrow Transplantation (CARE-BMT) score, with 68.9% categorized as low to moderate risk [6]. Although no formal cardiovascular risk assessment was reported in the PRADA II study, baseline comorbidities and the authors’ discussion indicate that most participants were likely at low to moderate cardiovascular risk [8]. The prevalence of hypertension at baseline ranged from 7.2% to 31.6% among the included studies. The mean cumulative doxorubicin equivalent dose ranged from 200 to 300 mg/m2 in 3 studies [7–9], and was below 200 mg/m2 in one study [6]. Follow-up duration ranged from 6 to 18 months. In the intervention group, one trial used a lower dose of sacubitril/valsartan (24.5/25.5 mg twice daily),7 whereas the other three studies up-titrated treatment to 97/103 mg twice daily, or the maximally tolerated dose. The baseline utilization of renin-angiotensin system inhibitors across the analyzed clinical trials exhibited certain heterogeneity. In the PRADA II and SARAH trials, the use of ACE inhibitors or ARBs was listed as an exclusion criterion [8, 9]. Similarly, RAS inhibitors were not employed in the control group of the study by Katogiannis et al.6 In contrast, the study by Hsu et al. included a small proportion of participants receiving ARBs, specifically 5.0% in the intervention group and 8.8% in the control group [7]. The impact of interventions on cancer therapy interruption was reported only in PRADA II trial.

sec.title: Result of the quality assessment
sec.p: The risk of bias for the four included randomized controlled trials was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool. Overall, the quality of the studies included was generally acceptable. However, two studies were not double-blinded during the randomization process, which resulted in some concerns regarding risk of bias [6, 7] (Supplementary Fig. 1). Specifically, the study of Hsu et al. employed an open-label design with blinded outcome assessment7, while the study of Katogiannis did not use a placebo tablet in the control group despite maintaining blinding during data acquisition and analysis [6]. These design features primarily affected the randomization domain (domain 1). Echocardiographic image analyses were conducted with blinding to study group allocation in all 4 included studies, resulting in a low risk of bias in outcome measurement.

sec.title: Primary endpoint – cancer therapy related cardiac dysfunction
sec.p: The incidence of CTRCD was reported in three studies, with 147 events within 350 participants [7–9]. The definition of CTRCD varied across studies. In the study by Hsu et al., CTRCD was defined according to the study’s original criteria, based on changes in LVEF or GLS (> 15% decline). All of the CTRCD events in the study of Hsu et al. were classified as mild. In the SARAH study, CTRCD was defined according to the study’s primary endpoint (> 15% decline in GLS). A secondary endpoint was defined as a decrease in LVEF > 10 to a final value < 53%, which was not fully aligned with 2022 ESC cardio-oncology guideline definitions (LVEF cutoff 50%) [2]. In the PRADA II study, CTRCD was defined according to the 2022 ESC cardio-oncology guidelines. The majority of CTRCD events in PRADA II was classified as mild (106/108, 98.1%), primarily driven by a GLS decline of > 15% or biomarker elevation. The pooled analysis showed that sacubitril/valsartan was associated with lower risk of CTRCD compared with controls (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.82, p < 0.001) (Fig. 2). There was substantial heterogeneity between the enrolled studies (I2 =68%, T2 = 0.542, p = 0.044). A sensitivity analysis with Bayesian method revealed a pooled RR of 0.76 (95% Credible Interval (CrI) 0.56 to 1.01); the probability of RR < 1 was 97.2% (Supplementary Figures S2A). A second sensitivity was conducted by using alternative criteria for CTRCD defined in PRADA II trial (clinically significant reduction in LVEF by 5% as assessed by CMR). The result showed that the sacubitril/valsartan was still associated with lower risk of CTRCD compared with controls (RR 0.54, 95% CI0.36 to 0.81, p = 0.003, Supplementary Figures S2B). Analysis stratified by CTRCD severity was not feasible due to the limited availability of relevant data in the included trials.

caption.p: Effect of sacubitril/valsartan on cancer therapy–related cardiac dysfunction. Forest plot illustrates the pooled effect of sacubitril/valsartan compared with control on the incidence of cancer therapy–related cardiac dysfunction. Effect estimates are presented as risk ratio with 95% confidence intervals. The study by Katogiannis et al. did not report CTRCD as a dichotomous endpoint and was not included in this analysis

sec.title: Key secondary endpoints – LVEF, GLS and cardiac troponin
sec.p: All four studies reported changes in LVEF from baseline to follow-up [6–9]. The pooled data showed significant increase in LVEF after sacubitril/valsartan treatment compared with control group: MD 1.19, 95% CI 0.05 to 2.33, p = 0.045. (Fig. 3) [6–9]. There was low heterogeneity for this outcome, as indicated by low I2 and T2 (I2 = 0, T2 = 0, p = 0.813). A sensitivity analysis excluding the study by Katogiannis et al., given its different participant population and lower cumulative doxorubicin-equivalent dose [6]. The result showed that the pooled effect remained statistically significant: MD 0.98, 95% CI 0.24 to 1.73, p = 0.029, with low heterogeneity (I2 = 0, T2 = 0, p = 0.905) (Supplementary Figures S3A).

caption.p: Effect of sacubitril/valsartan on left ventricular ejection fraction. Forest plot illustrates the effect of sacubitril/valsartan versus control on left ventricular ejection fraction. Pooled results are expressed as mean differences with 95% confidence intervals

sec.p: All four studies reported changes in GLS from baseline to follow-up [6–9]. Three studies assessed GLS using echocardiography systems from GE HealthCare [6–8], whereas one study used a Philips platform [9]. The pooled data from four studies that reported GLS change showed a significant increase in GLS after sacubitril/valsartan treatment: SMD 0.43, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.75 p = 0.026 (Fig. 4) [6–9]. There was low heterogeneity for this result (I2 = 0% and T2 < 0.0001, p = 0.410). A sensitivity analysis excluding the study of Katogiannis et al.6, showed no significant differences between sacubitril/valsartan treatment and control group: SMD 0.40, 95% CI − 0.19 to 0.99, p = 0.099, Supplementary Figures S3B.

caption.p: Effect of sacubitril/valsartan on global longitudinal strain. Forest plot illustrates the effect of sacubitril/valsartan compared with control on global longitudinal strain. Effect estimates are reported as standardized mean differences with 95% confidence intervals

sec.p: Cardiac troponin was assessed in all four studies [6–9]. Two studies measured hs-cTnT [6, 7], one measured hs-cTnI [9], and one (PRADA II) measured both hs-cTnI and hs-cTnT [8]. When both isoforms were available, hs-cTnI data were extracted for primary analysis. Pooled analysis of four studies demonstrated a significantly lower change in cardiac troponin levels in the sacubitril/valsartan group compared with the control group (log MD -0.43, 95% CI − 0.59 to − 0.26, p < 0.001, Fig. 5). There was low heterogeneity for this outcome (I2 =0, T2 <0.001, p = 0.396). A sensitivity analysis excluding the study by Katogiannis et al.6, showed similar benefit in sacubitril/valsartan treatment group: log MD − 0.39, 95% CI − 0.57 to – 0.21, p < 0.001, supplementary figure S4A). Two additional sensitivity tests were conducted using hs-cTnT from PRADA II trial: (1) including all four trials, and (2) further excluding the study of Katogiannis et al.6 The analysis including all four trials showed a significantly lower change in cardiac troponin (log MD -0.28, 95% CI − 0.53 to − 0.04, p = 0.024, supplementary figure S4B). However, this significance was not observed in the analysis excluding the study of Katogiannis et al. (log MD − 0.20, 95% CI − 0.45 to 0.04, p = 0.098, supplementary figure S4C).

caption.p: Effect of sacubitril/valsartan on troponin change. Forest plot illustrates the effect of sacubitril/valsartan versus control on changes in cardiac troponin levels. Pooled estimates are expressed as log–mean differences with 95% confidence intervals

sec.title: Exploratory endpoints – LV volumes and myocardial works
sec.p: Two trials (SARAH and Katogiannis et al.) evaluated the effects of sacubitril/valsartan on the change of LVESV and LVEDV [6–9]. Compared with control group, sacubitril/valsartan treatment did not result in a significant reduction in LVESV (MD − 3.68; 95% CI − 21.16 to 13.8; p = 0.563) or LVEDV (MD − 4.05; 95% CI − 66.93 to 58.84; p = 0.228, Supplementary figure S5A&B).

Two trials (Hsu et al. and Katogiannis et al.) reported changes in myocardial global work indices [6, 7]. Sacubitril/valsartan treatment was not associated with significant differences in any of the four myocardial global work indices compared with the control group, including global wasted work (GWW; MD − 46.1, 95% CI − 248.19 to 156.18; p = 0.212), global work efficiency (GWE; 2.26, 95% CI − 11.06 to 15.60; p = 0.277), global work index (GWI; 44.3, 95% CI − 1013 to 1102; p = 0.687), and global constructive work (GCW; −23.53, 95% CI − 1133 to 1085; p = 0.832) (Supplementary figure S5C-F). All included studies reported blood pressure outcomes [6–9]. The pooled analysis showed a significant reduction in DBP with sacubitril/valsartan treatment (MD − 4.06 mmHg; 95% CI − 8.01 to − 0.11; p = 0.047), whereas the reduction in SBP did not reach statistical significance (MD − 7.71 mmHg; 95% CI − 16.76 to 1.37; p = 0.074) (Supplementary figure S5G&H).

Three of the studies reported NT-proBNP [7–9]. The pooled analysis showed no significant reduction in NT-proBNP in sacubitril/valsartan group compared with control group (log-MD − 0.17 95% −0.51 to 0.17, p = 0.316, Supplementary figure S5I).

sec.title: Safety endpoint - hypotension
sec.p: The incidence of hypotension was reported in all four studies, with 22 events in 410 participants [6–9]. Sacubitril/valsartan was associated with significantly higher risk of hypotension compared with controls (RR 4.75, 95% CI 1.78 to 12.63, p = 0.002) (Fig. 6). There was low heterogeneity for this outcome (I2 = 0%, T2 = 0.067, p = 0.393). A sensitivity analysis with Bayesian method yielded a pooled RR of 4.45 (95% CrI 1.36 to 14.64). The probability of RR > 1 was 99.3% (Supplementary Figures S6A).

caption.p: Risk of hypotension associated with sacubitril/valsartan. Forest plot illustrates the association between sacubitril/valsartan use and the risk of hypotension. Effect estimates are presented as risk ratio with 95% confidence intervals

sec.title: Subgroup analysis
sec.p: A subgroup analysis based on the status of HER2 was performed. Two studies reported the change of LVEF in HER2 positive subgroup (PRADA II and SARAH) [8, 9]. However, the effect of sacubitril/valsartan on LVEF change in the subgroup of HER2 positive did not show significant difference compared with controls (MD 1.92, 95% CI − 19.68 to 23.52, p = 0.461). (Supplementary Figure S7).

sec.title: Trial sequential analysis (TSA)
sec.p: TSA for CTRCD showed that although the pooled estimate reached conventional statistical significance, the accrued sample size (n = 350) did not meet the diversity-adjusted required information size, and the cumulative Z-curve did not cross the trial sequential monitoring boundary (Supplementary Figure S8). These findings indicate that the current evidence remains insufficient to confirm a definitive treatment effect. Therefore, current results should be considered hypothesis-generating rather than sufficient to inform clinical practice.

sec.title: Publication bias
sec.p: Funnel plots for each outcome are presented in Supplementary Figure S9. Because only four studies were included, Egger’s tests were not performed.

sec.title: Main findings
sec.p: Our meta-analysis yields the following findings. First, among patients with preserved baseline cardiac function, the use of sacubitril/valsartan was associated with a lower incidence of CTRCD compared with control. Second, in line with the observed reduction in CTRCD, sacubitril/valsartan therapy was associated with modest but statistically significant attenuation of declines in LVEF and GLS, whereas differences in myocardial work indices were less consistent, possibly reflecting limited data and methodological heterogeneity. Third, sacubitril/valsartan use was associated with reduced myocardial injury, as evidenced by smaller increases in troponin levels, supporting a potential cardioprotective effect at the subclinical level. Fourth, sacubitril/valsartan treatment was accompanied by a significantly higher incidence of hypotension. Finally, trial sequential analysis indicated that the cumulative Z-curve did not cross the monitoring boundary and that the required information size has not been reached, suggesting that the current evidence remains insufficient. Taken together, these findings are primarily driven by imaging-based and biomarker-derived surrogate endpoints and do not yet support definitive conclusions regarding clinical benefit.

CTRCD was selected as the main endpoint in the present study, because a considerable proportion of cardiotoxicity related to contemporary cancer therapies presents as asymptomatic deterioration in cardiac function, which would be underestimated if only symptomatic heart failure were considered. Importantly, CTRCD can be identified at asymptomatic stage prior to the development of overt heart failure, thereby providing an opportunity for earlier intervention and closer surveillance [1]. The reported incidence of CTRCD varies widely, ranging from approximately 10% to 67%, in part reflecting differences in diagnostic criteria and surveillance strategies across studies [12, 13]. The 2022 ESC cardio-oncology guidelines propose a comprehensive definition of CTRCD that integrates cardiac imaging (including LVEF and GLS) and cardiac biomarkers (troponin and natriuretic peptides), which facilitates standardized outcome assessment across studies [2]. Among the three trials included in the CTRCD analysis, GLS was incorporated into the definition of CTRCD in all three studies. In contrast, cardiac troponin was included in the CTRCD definition according to the 2022 ESC guidelines only in PRADA II, but not in the other two trials. Accordingly, the reported incidence of CTRCD may vary across studies. Furthermore, TSA indicated that the accumulated evidence has not yet reached the required information size. Therefore, these findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than conclusive, given the limited number of available trials.

In our meta-analysis, sacubitril/valsartan were associated with a modest but statistically significant attenuation of LVEF decline in the preventive cardio-oncology setting. The effects of other neurohormonal preventive strategies on LVEF, particularly renin–angiotensin system inhibitors and beta-blockers, have been examined in prior meta-analyses. In a meta-analysis including studies of patients with various malignancies, treatment with ACEI, ARB or beta-blockers was associated with a favorable change in LVEF of 3.96% compared with control, albeit with considerable heterogeneity [14]. In another meta-analysis including studies of patients with breast cancer receiving anthracycline and trastuzumab therapy, treatment with ACEI, ARB or beta-blockers is also associated with favorable LVEF change of 2.0% compared with control group. However, subgroup analyses restricted to ACEIs or ARBs did not demonstrate a statistically significant difference between the treatment and control groups [15]. A recent meta-analysis including studies of patients receiving anthracycline therapy found that treatment with ACEI or ARB did not reduce CTRCD but with favorable changes in LVEF and LV volume indices [16]. Another meta-analysis on the effect of statin on LVEF included 5 RCTs and revealed a mean difference of 1.88% LVEF, with considerable heterogeneity [17]. Our analysis demonstrated a small but statistically significant effect of sacubitril/valsartan on LVEF, with an estimated effect size of MD 1.19% or SMD 0.25, and low between-study heterogeneity (I² = 0%). The use of ACEI/ARB or beta-blocker was limited or excluded from the four trials included in our analysis, therefore direct comparative effectiveness between sacubitril/valsartan and these agents could not be assessed.

GLS has only recently been proposed as a diagnostic criterion for CTRCD and, as a result, has not been routinely assessed in prior meta-analyses of preventive neurohormonal strategies. In a meta-analysis by Vaduganathan et al., preventive treatment with ARBs or beta-blockers was associated with a small-to-modest improvement in global longitudinal strain, based on a pooled analysis of three trials (SMD − 0.43).14 These findings are consistent with our results, in which a similar magnitude of effect was observed (SMD 0.43), corresponding to an approximate absolute change of 1.1% in GLS. According to a previous review, a 10 to 15% relative reduction (2 to 3% absolute change in GLS) during cancer therapy can predict the development of cardiotoxicity [18]. However, the clinical utility of GLS-guided cardioprotection remains uncertain. In the SUCCOUR trial, a GLS-guided strategy increased the use of cardioprotective therapies but did not result in a significant improvement in long-term left ventricular ejection fraction compared with an LVEF-guided approach [19]. Therefore, there is currently insufficient evidence to support that GLS-based preventive strategies translate into meaningful clinical benefit. Taken together, these findings suggest that sacubitril/valsartan is associated with statistically significant but modest improvements in LVEF and GLS following cancer therapy, and whether these changes translate into clinically relevant outcomes warrants further investigation.

Our results further indicate that sacubitril/valsartan treatment is associated with attenuated myocardial injury, in parallel with its protective effects on left ventricular function. The protective effects of neurohormonal preventive strategies, other than sacubitril/valsartan, on myocardial injury in the context of CTRCD have been evaluated in prior meta-analyses. One meta-analysis included eleven RCTs, and beta-blocker therapy was associated with a significantly lower risk of cardiac troponin I elevation above 0.04 ng/mL [20]. Similar results have also been noted for ACEI and ARB [21]. In the same analysis on the prediction power of troponin, troponins were predictive of CTRCD in patients receiving cytotoxic chemotherapies. Troponin has been proposed as a monitoring tool with high negative predictive value and also be a marker for the efficacy of preventive strategies [21]. Taken together, sacubitril/valsartan appears to attenuate myocardial injury in CTRCD, consistent with prior evidence on neurohormonal blockade, with cardiac troponin providing supporting mechanistic evidence.

Myocardial work indices are considered relatively load-independent parameters. However, their role in the early detection of CTRCD, particularly in comparison with GLS, remains controversial [22]. In the present analysis, no significant differences in the change of myocardial work indices were observed between the two study groups. Notably, only two studies included in our analysis reported myocardial work indices, and these studies exhibited marked heterogeneity in sex distribution, with one study enrolling only women and the other comprising a predominantly male population (63% men). This heterogeneity and the small study number may limit the generalizability of the findings.

Our analysis showed a higher risk of hypotension with sacubitril/valsartan treatment compared with control. This was consistent with a significant reduction in diastolic blood pressure of approximately 4 mmHg. However, the clinical impact of hypotension was not assessed in the included studies, and therefore its relevance to clinically relevant outcomes remain uncertain. Given the modest and clinically uncertain benefits observed, these findings warrant careful consideration when evaluating the overall benefit–risk balance of sacubitril/valsartan as a preventive strategy for CTRCD.

sec.title: Implications
sec.p: 2022 ESC guidelines recommended several primary prevention strategies for high and very high-risk patients, including ACEI/ARB, beta-blocker, dexrazoxane and statin (all class IIa indication), in addition to minimizing the use of cardiotoxic drugs [2]. Although our results showed that ARNI was associated with a lower incidence of CTRCD and modest improvements in LVEF, GLS, and myocardial injury, the clinical relevance of these findings warrants cautious interpretation. Trial sequential analysis further indicated that the current evidence remains insufficient, and the required information size has not been reached, limiting the ability to draw definitive conclusions. It remains uncertain whether these functional improvements will translate into reductions in heart failure hospitalization or major adverse cardiovascular events. In addition, the higher incidence of hypotension with sacubitril/valsartan warrants careful consideration of the balance between efficacy and tolerability. Taken together, current findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and not sufficient to change current clinical practice.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: Several limitations of this study should be noted. First, the number of included studies was small, with only four eligible trials meeting the inclusion criteria. This limited sample size reduces the statistical power of the meta-analysis and precludes robust subgroup or meta-regression analyses. Second, substantial heterogeneity existed in study design and methodology. Cardiac function was assessed using different imaging modalities (CMR and echocardiography), which may introduce variability in the detection and quantification of cardiac dysfunction. In addition, the enrolled populations were heterogeneous, with some studies including all risk level of cancer patients, while others selectively enrolled higher-risk patients, as identified by elevated troponin levels. As a result, analyses restricted to higher-risk populations, which may be more clinically relevant, were not feasible due to limited available data. Furthermore, the heterogeneity in cancer treatment regimens across the trials, including accumulative dosages and regimens, may exert different cardiotoxic stress. Moreover, three studies focused on patients with breast cancer, whereas one study included patients undergoing bone marrow transplantation, potentially limiting the generalizability of the findings to other cancer types and treatment settings. Another limitation is the lack of studies directly comparing ARNI and ARB, which would be clinically meaningful, thereby precluding formal comparative evaluation in this meta-analysis. Finally, the outcomes were restricted to CTRCD, a surrogate endpoint reflecting cardiac dysfunction, and no hard clinical outcomes such as heart failure hospitalization, cardiovascular mortality, or all-cause mortality were evaluated. Notably, the impact of the intervention on cancer therapy interruption, which may lead to adverse outcomes, was not assessed. Therefore, the clinical implications of the observed effects on long-term cardiovascular outcomes remain uncertain.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Sacubitril/valsartan treatment may be associated with a modest reduction in CTRCD risk and attenuation of LVEF and GLS decline, as well as lower markers of myocardial injury among patients with preserved baseline cardiac function receiving chemotherapy. However, the clinical relevance remains inconclusive when considering the trial sequential analysis, the modest magnitude of effect and the risk of hypotension. These findings should therefore be interpreted with caution and considered hypothesis-generating rather than practice-changing. Larger randomized trials incorporating clinically relevant endpoints, such as heart failure events, cancer therapy interruption, and cardiovascular outcomes, are needed to clarify the potential role of ARNI in preventive strategies, particularly in higher-risk populations.
